html:
Introduction

For millions of people, food is an integral part of a train journey. Long-distance travel often means purchasing meals, snacks, beverages, or other food items during the journey.

But an important question deserves attention:

How safe is the food we eat during a train journey?

Food safety depends on much more than how the food looks or tastes. It involves hygiene during preparation, safe storage, temperature control, transportation, handling, and protection from contamination.

Food-safety violations and passenger complaints about food quality highlight the importance of maintaining strict food-safety standards throughout the railway food-supply chain. At the same time, it is important to recognize that not all railway food is unsafe; authorised catering systems and regulated food businesses are subject to food-safety requirements and monitoring. (IRCTC eCatering⁠￼)

Why Is Food Safety Particularly Important During Train Journeys?

Food can become contaminated at multiple stages—from preparation and storage to transportation and serving.

Microorganisms such as bacteria, viruses, and parasites can contaminate food when hygiene practices are inadequate.

Improper temperature control is another important concern. Perishable foods can support the growth of harmful microorganisms when they are kept for prolonged periods at temperatures that allow bacterial multiplication.

Contamination can also occur through:

* Unclean hands
* Contaminated utensils
* Unsafe water
* Improper food storage
* Cross-contamination between raw and cooked foods
* Inadequate cleaning of preparation surfaces
* Exposure to dust, insects, or other environmental contaminants

Therefore, food safety is a process that begins before the food reaches the passenger.

The Importance of Food Handling

Even food that was initially prepared safely can become contaminated through improper handling.

Food handlers should maintain appropriate personal hygiene, use clean utensils, and prevent contact between raw and cooked foods.

Ready-to-eat foods require particular care because they may be consumed without another cooking step that could reduce microbial contamination.

During a train journey, additional challenges can arise because food may need to be transported, stored, reheated, and served in a moving environment.

Temperature Control Matters

Temperature is one of the most important factors in food safety.

FSSAI guidance recommends appropriate temperature control for high-risk foods, including keeping hot foods sufficiently hot and cold foods appropriately chilled. Food that is transported or displayed should also be protected from contamination and excessive holding time. (FSSAI⁠￼)

This is particularly relevant for foods containing ingredients such as meat, poultry, seafood, eggs, dairy products, and cooked foods.

A meal may look perfectly normal while still containing harmful microorganisms.

Appearance and taste alone cannot reliably determine whether food is microbiologically safe.

What About Unauthorised Vendors?

One important concern during railway travel is purchasing food from unauthorised vendors.

Unauthorised vending on Indian Railways is prohibited, and railway authorities conduct inspections and special drives to address unauthorised vending. The railway system has also introduced measures such as identity verification for authorised catering personnel. (Press Information Bureau⁠￼)

Buying food through authorised channels provides greater accountability and allows passengers to use established complaint and customer-support mechanisms.

IRCTC eCatering advises passengers to use its official eCatering platform, Food on Track application, and authorised partners when ordering food during train journeys. (IRCTC eCatering⁠￼)

This does not mean that every authorised outlet is automatically perfect, but regulated and authorised food services provide a stronger framework for food-safety oversight.

Food Poisoning: What Can Happen?

Contaminated food can cause foodborne illness.

Depending on the causative organism or toxin, symptoms may include:

* Nausea
* Vomiting
* Abdominal cramps
* Diarrhoea
* Fever
* Weakness
* Dehydration

Most healthy adults recover from many uncomplicated episodes of foodborne illness, but some infections can become serious.

Young children, older adults, pregnant women, and people with certain underlying medical conditions may be particularly vulnerable to severe foodborne disease.

Why “It Looks Fresh” Is Not Enough

One of the common misconceptions about food safety is that unsafe food will always smell bad, look spoiled, or taste unusual.

This is not necessarily true.

Some pathogenic microorganisms can multiply without producing obvious changes in appearance, smell, or taste.

Therefore, visual inspection can provide some information about obvious spoilage, but it cannot guarantee microbiological safety.

What Can Passengers Do?

Passengers can reduce unnecessary food-safety risks by making sensible choices during travel.

Whenever possible:

* Purchase food from authorised and regulated sources.
* Prefer freshly prepared food that is appropriately hot when it is supposed to be served hot.
* Avoid food that appears improperly stored or handled.
* Be cautious with highly perishable foods that have been kept at inappropriate temperatures.
* Avoid consuming food with obvious spoilage, contamination, damaged packaging, or an unusual appearance.
* Maintain hand hygiene before eating.
* Use safe drinking water.

These measures cannot eliminate every foodborne risk, but they can reduce avoidable exposure.

The Responsibility Does Not Belong Only to the Passenger

Food safety is not simply a matter of consumers being careful.

Food providers, caterers, vendors, food handlers, regulatory authorities, and railway management all have important responsibilities.

Food should be sourced appropriately, prepared hygienically, stored at safe temperatures, transported safely, and served under conditions that minimize contamination.

FSSAI requires food businesses to implement appropriate food-safety management systems and good hygiene practices throughout the food chain. (FSSAI⁠￼)

Regular inspection, monitoring, enforcement, food-safety training, and effective complaint mechanisms are essential components of a safe food system.

Conclusion

A train journey should not require passengers to compromise on food safety.

Food can become contaminated at multiple points between preparation and consumption, and factors such as hygiene, temperature control, storage, transportation, and handling all influence its safety.

Passengers should therefore prefer food from authorised and regulated sources and avoid purchasing food from unauthorised vendors where the conditions of preparation and storage cannot be adequately verified.

At the same time, responsibility for food safety cannot rest entirely on passengers. Strong regulatory oversight, proper food-handling practices, routine inspections, and accountability throughout the railway food-supply chain are equally important.

The goal is not to create fear about eating during a train journey. It is to encourage better food hygiene, stronger accountability, and safer choices for every railway passenger.
